newsitem.title: USA: Clinton unlikely to rock the boat at Fed --experts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unlikely to rock the boat at Fed --experts.

text.p: President Clinton, fresh from a reelection victory that he owes in part to the Federal Reserve for its deft handling of the economy, will likely maintain a hands-off stance toward the central bank.

In contrast to the Bush administration, which actively lobbied for low interest rates in the 1992 election year, a trademark of the Clinton administration has been its tendency to refrain from attempting to strong-arm the independent Fed.

Such a policy has been well-received among policymakers at the central bank. San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry commended the administration in an interview this year for making "every effort not to be intrusive."
Few analysts expect that policy to change in a second Clinton term.
"President Clinton's administration has been extremely hands-off toward the Fed, more so than other administration in recent memory," said David Wyss, research director at DRI/McGraw-Hill.

"In a sense the reasoning is circular," Wyss said. "Since the economy has been doing so well, there is no need to pressure the Fed. But part of the reason the economy is doing so well is the administration has left the Fed to do what it needs to do."

Analysts credit the Fed, led by Alan Greenspan, with keeping the economy on an even keel by administering a needed dose of higher interest rates in 1994 and early 1995 when the economy appeared set to overheat. It later changed course when growth began to flag.

The result gave Clinton and his advisers plenty to brag about this election year. The economy is growing solidly while unemployment at 5.2 percent is close to a seven-year low and inflation is hovering near a mild 3 percent.
"The hands-off strategy has paid great dividends," said Lyle Gramley, a former Fed governor who is now a consulting economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.
Gramley and other analysts attribute the strategy of not meddling with monetary policy to Clinton's Treasury Secretary, Robert Rubin, a former Wall Street trader.

The logic is that attempts to pressure the Fed on short-term interest rates are rarely successful and are often counterproductive because they tend to spook the bond market, thus sending long-term rates higher.

"It has become clear to the administration that it's important to take into account the bond market," said economist Kurt Karl of the WEFA Group. "They seem to understand quite well that the best way to get lower interest rates is to pursue a hands-off policy."
A notable exception to the tendency toward restraint came earlier this year when Clinton urged a debate at the Fed on whether to allow faster growth.

Attempting to further that debate, the White House floated the name of pro-growth investment banker Felix Rohatyn for the vacant vice chairman's seat but later withdrew it in the face of Senate Republican opposition.

Although several members of Congress have also picked up the pro-growth mantle, most observers believe Congress too will do little to try to pressure the central bank, particularly with Fed-friendly Republicans such as Rep. Jim Leach (R-Iowa) heading key committees such as the House Banking panel.
Concerning the impact of a second Clinton term on the makeup of the Fed, few expect that to change much either.

Greenspan, whose inflation-fighting credentials are highly respected, was reappointed by Clinton earlier this year. The president also named Fed Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin and two current governors, Janet Yellen and Laurence Meyer.

"My sense is that Clinton will look for people who are concerned about economic growth," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute think tank. But he added that overall, any Clinton appointees are likely to hold "moderate, middle-of-the-road views" similar to those of the appointees already named by the president.
